1.story: Tanya Russell's bronze shows a child holding a dog's face. Lord David Blunkett unveiled it on 23 October 2026 to mark the Archbishop's Park Community Trust's 25th anniversary and its work improving the park.

2.story: These paired hounds connect Victoria Park with the classical Molossian dog tradition. Historic England records Lady Regnart's donation in 1912 and restoration in 1991. Keep these distinct from the ancient Jennings Dog in the British Museum; the shared Alcibiades name does not make them the same object.

3.story: Hector sits beside shipowner and philanthropist Richard Green in Edward William Wyon's monument, erected in 1866. London Remembers relates that the missing ear was cut away to free a boy trapped while climbing it. Treat that incident as the source's reported story rather than independently established fact.

4.story: The present terrier is Nicola Hicks's 1985 replacement memorial, relocated within Battersea Park in 1992. It commemorates the earlier Brown Dog monument, removed in 1910; photographs and histories of the original refer to a different sculpture.

5.story: Gillie and Marc's camera-carrying dogs turn the act of looking at public art back onto the visitor. The artists' current listing places this group in Norfolk Square Gardens; its Royal Exchange URL records an earlier location. Confirm the group on site before visiting.

6.story: Dickens remembered a golden dog licking a pot on his childhood walk home. The modern elm replicas are Edward and Bill: Edward was unveiled in 2013, removed after weather damage in 2025, and replaced by gilded Bill on 7 February 2026, unveiled by Dickens's descendant Ollie Dickens.

7.story: Delve based this sleeping-dog bench on its office whippet Rocket for the 2019 London Festival of Architecture. The design links taking a rest with the support dogs offer mental health. The maker records its later move to Centre Point, near the Arcade entrance on New Oxford Street.

8.story: Lion is a mastiff, despite his name. He guards bare-knuckle boxer Tom Sayers's tomb, dating from around 1865. Historic England reports that the dog rode in his own open carriage immediately behind the coffin at Sayers's funeral. Check West Cemetery admission arrangements.

9.story: The memorial honours animals used in war. A bronze dog and horse emerge beyond the wall, while burdened mules approach from the other side. The composition lets visitors follow the animals' journey through the monument; it is not a memorial to one named pet.

10.story: This dog drinking fountain commemorates actor Esme Percy. The Royal Parks management plan dates the bronze on a granite pedestal to 1961 and credits Silvia Gilley; other catalogues spell the sculptor's first name Sylvia. No checked source establishes that the bronze portrays Percy's own dog.

11.story: Jonathan Wylder's Talbot dogs form part of the first Marquess of Westminster monument commissioned in 1998. The dogs refer to heraldic supporters on the Westminster coat of arms and an extinct type of hound. The artist's gallery places the original at Wilton Crescent and Belgrave Square; refine the CSV's garden-level search pin.

12.story: Bashaw was the Earl of Dudley's Newfoundland. The Earl commissioned Matthew Cotes Wyatt to portray his favourite dog but died before the work was completed. The V&A records the lavish materials and John Ruskin's later hostile criticism: a private pet portrait became a conspicuous argument about artistic taste. Check current museum display before visiting.

13.story: This Roman marble dog probably follows a lost Greek bronze. Henry Jennings linked its damaged tail to Plutarch's story of Alcibiades cutting his dog's tail to distract public gossip. That is the history of its nickname, not proof it depicts Alcibiades's actual dog. The British Museum acquired it after a public campaign in 2001.

14.story: Jim Mathieson's Hogarth monument was unveiled on Chiswick High Road in October 2001. Trump, Hogarth's pug, sits at the painter's feet; the William Hogarth Trust describes the dog as part of the statue's unveiling. A useful story is the artist's attachment to a dog remembered alongside him in public.

15.story: Elisabeth Frink made this bronze in 1958; it reached its intended Cranbrook Estate setting in 1963. The pairing of a vulnerable man and his dog gives a human focus to the estate's public space. Historic England lists it in its own right, so retain the sculptural group as one candidate.

16.story: Stephen Bunn's dog-and-kennel sculpture makes a literal connection to Dog Kennel Hill. The April 1993 Sainsbury staff journal documents the work in connection with the development, giving an early contemporary source beyond a modern map pin. Confirm its current condition and exact St Francis Park position.

17.story: Kew's greyhound belongs to the Queen's Beasts, heraldic animals representing royal ancestry. James Woodford made the original plaster beasts for Elizabeth II's 1953 coronation; Kew's outdoor set follows that tradition. This is a heraldic dog rather than a portrait of a named pet, and a separate object from the Hampton Court versions.

18.story: The White Greyhound of Richmond is one of Hampton Court's Tudor beasts on the Moat Bridge. These animals advertise royal lineage and legitimacy, functioning as dynastic emblems. Keep this bridge sculpture separate from the painted oak greyhound in Chapel Court and Kew's Queen's Beasts.

19.story: Chapel Court was recreated in 2009 for the 500th anniversary of Henry VIII's accession. Its eight English-oak beasts evoke Tudor royal imagery, including the White Greyhound of Richmond. The garden draws on a court portrait and early heraldic drawings; this is a modern recreation, not an intact Tudor dog carving.

20.story: Hounslow's proposed local heritage list identifies the wooden dog as representing Gunnersbury Park's use by dog walkers. That provides a local everyday-life story, but the checked material does not establish a sculptor, date or named dog. Those details and the current condition need further research.

21.story: This Kongo nkisi is a ritual object, not a pet memorial. The British Museum explains that dogs connect village life with the forest and the dead; Kozo's two heads strengthen that mediating role. Medicines empower the figure for a ritual specialist. Preserve that cultural context when writing about it and confirm current display.

22.story: The giant Nipper connects the regenerated Old Vinyl Factory with its record-making history. Masterplanners Studio Egret West describe Nipper, gramophone sculptures and record-shaped street furniture as ways to tell that history throughout the site. Their accounts describe a roughly six-metre/20-foot statue; the CSV's 5.5-metre figure should not be treated as an exact measurement.

23.story: The dogs appear in Paul Day's intimate relief of the Queen Mother's interests, part of the 2009 memorial with Philip Jackson's standing statue. The relief contrasts private life with the other panel's wartime scenes. The CSV names the corgis Rush and Minnie; that identification is also reported by Monumental Tales, rather than specified on the artist's page.

24.story: Rabbitwoman and Dogman ride together in Gillie and Marc's interactive tandem. The artists connect it with their own shared travels and the cooperation needed to ride tandem, inviting a visitor onto the spare seat. Their current page lists Canary Wharf as a permanent exhibition.

25.story: The spare seat between Dogman and Rabbitwoman invites strangers into their friendship. The artists frame the unlikely animal pairing as acceptance of differences. Their current location is 7 Cavendish Square; Battersea Power Station and Lowndes Square are past installations, despite the old Halkin Arcade URL.

26.story: Rabbitwoman steers a Vespa while Dogman rides in the sidecar. The artists relate the design to travelling together and trusting a partner, with a spare place for a visitor. The current listing is Spitalfields, 101 Commercial Street; the Brunswick Centre in the URL is an earlier location.

27.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman host endangered animals at a bronze banquet, leaving seats for people to join them. The artists use the gathering to connect hospitality with wildlife protection. Their page now lists Eastbourne Terrace in Paddington and records Paternoster Square as a past exhibition.

28.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman lift a rhino in Gillie and Marc's conservation design. Kingston's organiser lists Rise Up Rhino outside TK Maxx within Wild Kingston, advertised until September 2026. That end date has passed: current presence is unconfirmed and this must not yet be treated as a reliable visit destination.

29.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman plant flowers, shrubs and trees to restore wildlife habitat.

30.story: In the artists' fictional scene, Dogman and Rabbitwoman haul an elephant to safety. The action asks people to help threatened elephants rather than stand aside.

31.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman choose a shared skateboard as a low-emission way to go adventuring. The artists use this playful transport solution to connect pleasure with environmental responsibility.

32.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman invent a game with a basketball. The artists connect playful experimentation with creativity and finding fresh solutions in everyday life.

33.story: Rabbitwoman peers out of a manhole and calls down to Dogman. Their climb becomes the artists' fictional lesson about effort, discovery and enjoying a new perspective.

34.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman share a modest home with visiting friends; companionship matters more than grandeur.

35.story: The artists imagine Dogman and Rabbitwoman meeting an elephant in a tree. She is a former circus performer celebrating freedom; the unlikely encounter becomes a friendship story, not a documented animal biography.

36.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman photograph adventures to preserve moments they can enjoy again.

37.story: This stop belongs to the artists' Little Things trail about the wider effect of small acts of kindness and care. An individual narrative for the exact title A Little Recycle was not established in the checked catalogue; confirm the depicted characters and plaque on site rather than borrow another sculpture's story.

38.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman pause together on a bench, valuing quiet company over grand adventures.

39.story: The artists imagine Dogman and Rabbitwoman progressing patiently without shortcuts. Their journey stands for accepting gradual change rather than rushing toward a destination.

40.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman treat friendship as chosen family, giving encouragement and practical support and receiving it in return. This miniature and A Little Step at a Time share an address but are distinct artworks.

41.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman show friends that small gestures of care can brighten a difficult day.

42.story: The artists imagine Dogman and Rabbitwoman in a town where people help one another and listen equally to everyone's ideas. The story presents everyday support as the foundation of community happiness.

43.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman tackle litter themselves, encouraging others to join the clean-up.

44.story: Rabbitwoman promotes reuse and recycling while Dogman picks up litter: small practical actions protect their surroundings.

45.story: Dogman and Rabbitwoman find an abandoned egg and keep it warm in a nest. The artists' fictional adoption story links caring for vulnerable wildlife with the happiness of helping another life.

46.story: Giro was German diplomat Leopold von Hoesch's dog, buried in the former embassy garden after dying in 1934. Atlas Obscura reports accidental electrocution, which should remain an attributed account. This is a grave marker rather than a dog sculpture; avoid presenting it as the grave of a dog owned by Hitler.

47.story: Patrick McEvoy's playful dog bench memorialised a pampered dachshund looked after by his housemates. London Remembers quotes his account that the memorial was premature, so the inscription should not be used as a factual death record. Its listing is marked lost; retain this as an archived historical lead.
